etymology: From Saxon byldan, to construct a dwelling, from bold, a house. Hebrew banah means to build, and the noun bēn, a son, comes from the same root — a man builds his house by his children, which is why Scripture says a barren woman is built up when the LORD gives her a son.
biblical_def: Building in Scripture is never merely construction; it is the making of something meant to last, and the first question is always whose work it is. The Psalm states the governing principle in one line: “Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it” (Psalm 127:1) — not a discouragement of labour but a denial that labour is sufficient. The Lord Jesus claims the building of His own house and guarantees the outcome: “upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18) — the church is His project, and its permanence is His promise, not the builders'. Paul, having laid a foundation, warns every man who works on it: “let every man take heed how he buildeth thereupon” (1 Corinthians 3:10), and the fire of the day of judgment will test the material. And Nehemiah gives the human side of the work its finest sentence: “So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof: for the people had a mind to work” (Nehemiah 4:6). Set together these four texts form the whole doctrine of Christian labour: God builds or nothing stands; Christ builds His church infallibly; men build on His foundation answerably; and the people who actually get walls finished are the people with a mind to work.
webster_summary: To construct, erect, or raise, as an edifice; to establish and increase. In Scripture, the vanity of building without the LORD, Christ's promise to build His church against which hell shall not prevail, the warning to take heed how a man builds on the foundation, and the wall built by a people with a mind to work.
webster_full: BUILD, v.t. 1. To frame, construct and raise, as an edifice or fabric of almost any kind.
2. To raise by art; to frame or shape into a particular form; as, to build a ship.
3. To increase and strengthen; to cement or unite; to establish; as, to build up a family or a church.
4. From Saxon byldan, to build, from bold, a dwelling; Hebrew banah, to build.
5. In Scripture, except the LORD build the house, Ps. 127; upon this rock I will build my church, Matt. 16.
corruption_summary: Church growth is treated as a construction problem to be solved by method, so that what men build is credited to God; and Matthew 16:18 is bent into a claim for one bishop's successors rather than a promise about Christ's own work.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome reads Matthew 16:18 as the charter of the papacy: Peter is the rock, the office is perpetual, and the bishop of Rome inherits it. The text will not carry the weight. The Lord addresses Peter by the name He had given him and then shifts the word — thou art Petros, and upon this petra I will build — and the New Testament everywhere identifies the foundation otherwise: other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 3:11), and the household of God is built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ Himself being the chief corner stone (Ephesians 2:20). Peter himself, writing later, calls Christ the living stone and every believer a stone in the building, and never hints at a successor. The confession Peter had just made — Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God — is what the church is built on, and it is the promise, not the office, that hell cannot prevail against.

The practical corruption is nearer to most churches than the papal one. Where growth is treated as a technique — the right programme, the right music, the right demographic study — a congregation may be built rapidly and be built of wood, hay, and stubble. Paul does not forbid care in building; he commands it, telling every man to take heed how he builds, which assumes real responsibility and real skill. What he denies is that the work will escape testing. The fire shall try every man's work of what sort it is, and a man may be saved yet suffer loss with a lifetime's building burnt at his feet. The principle to recover joins Psalm 127 to Nehemiah 4: labour without God is vain, and God's building nevertheless goes up through people who have a mind to work.
roots_summary: Hebrew banah, to build, and by figure to establish a family; binyan, a building; Greek oikodomeō, to build a house, whence oikodomē, edification.
roots_lines: Hebrew banah (H1129) — to build, rebuild, establish; also used of God building Eve from Adam's rib (Genesis 2:22).
Hebrew bēn (H1121) — a son; from the same root as banah, since sons are how a house is built.
Greek oikodomeō (G3618) — to build a house; used of Christ building His church and of believers edifying one another.
Greek oikodomē (G3619) — a building, and figuratively edification; “ye are God's building” (1 Corinthians 3:9).
Greek themelios (G2310) — a foundation; the foundation laid by the wise masterbuilder (1 Corinthians 3:10-11).

Of Christ's indestructible work: upon this rock I will build my church (Matthew 16:18).
Of accountable workmanship: let every man take heed how he buildeth thereupon (1 Corinthians 3:10).

etymology: From Latin planta, a sprout or slip, and plantare, to set in the ground with the sole of the foot. Hebrew nata' means to fix or fasten in, and is used of trees, of vineyards, of tent pegs, and of a people settled in a land God has given them.
biblical_def: To plant is to put something where it will draw life from ground it did not choose, and Scripture makes the figure carry the doctrine of election, of nurture, and of judgment. The blessed man of the first Psalm is not self-supporting: he “shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season” (Psalm 1:3) — planted, passive, and therefore fruitful in due time. The Lord Jesus applies the same figure to false religion with terrible economy: “Every plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted, shall be rooted up” (Matthew 15:13) — the test is not vigour or reputation but origin. Paul distributes the labour and reserves the outcome: “I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:6) — a sentence that has kept many a minister sane. And Jeremiah is commissioned with the whole vocabulary of demolition and cultivation at once: set “over the nations and over the kingdoms, to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down, to build, and to plant” (Jeremiah 1:10) — four verbs of tearing down before the two of building, which is the usual order of God's work in a man and in a nation. Planting is God's prerogative; watering is the servant's duty; and increase is never anyone's achievement.
webster_summary: To put in the ground and cover, as seed or a slip, for growth; to set, fix, or establish. In Scripture, the man planted by rivers of water, every plant not planted by the Father rooted up, Paul planting and Apollos watering while God gives the increase, and the prophet set to pull down and to plant.
webster_full: PLANT, v.t. 1. To put in the ground and cover, as seed for growth; to set, as a shrub or tree.
2. To engender; to set the first inhabitants; to settle; as, to plant a colony.
3. To fix; to establish; as, to plant a church or an institution.
4. From Latin planta, a slip or shoot, and plantare, to set with the foot.
5. In Scripture, like a tree planted by the rivers of water, Ps. 1; I have planted, Apollos watered, 1 Cor. 3.
corruption_summary: Increase is credited to the labourer, so that ministerial success becomes a measure of the man; and the test of a religious movement becomes its growth rather than whether the Father planted it.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 15:13 supplies a criterion the age has almost entirely abandoned. Confronted with a religious system that was flourishing, respected, and hostile to Him, the Lord did not ask whether it was growing; He asked who planted it, and pronounced its end. Modern evaluation reverses the test. A movement that draws crowds, plants campuses, and reports numbers is presumed to have God's blessing on it, and to question it is treated as envy. But Scripture repeatedly shows error growing fast and truth held by a remnant — four hundred prophets of Baal against one Micaiah, a whole nation against Jeremiah, the multitude crying crucify him. Growth proves that something is being planted; it does not prove who planted it. The examination has to be doctrinal, and the fruit that finally tells is the fruit of the Spirit and of sound teaching, not attendance.

The second error attaches the increase to the man. Paul had every ground for taking credit at Corinth — he founded the church, he suffered for it, he loved it — and he refuses the credit in the plainest terms: neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase. This is not modesty; it is theology, and it cuts both ways for the labourer. It forbids him to boast when the field flourishes, and it forbids him to despair when it does not, because the increase was never in his hands. The principle to recover is that faithfulness in planting and watering is the whole of a servant's duty, and the harvest is the Lord's business. Where that is believed, ministers stop competing and start working.
roots_summary: Hebrew nata', to plant or fix in; matta', a plantation or that which is planted; Greek phyteuō, to plant, and phyteia, a planting or plant.
roots_lines: Hebrew nata' (H5193) — to plant, fasten, establish; used of vineyards, of Eden, and of Israel planted in the land.
Hebrew matta' (H4302) — a plantation, or a plant; “the planting of the LORD, that he might be glorified” (Isaiah 61:3).
Hebrew shathal (H8362) — to transplant; the verb of Psalm 1:3, a tree deliberately set beside water.
Greek phyteuō (G5452) — to plant; used of Paul's founding labour at Corinth (1 Corinthians 3:6).
Greek phyteia (G5451) — a planting, a plant; “every plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted” (Matthew 15:13).
usage: Of the fruitful believer's dependence: like a tree planted by the rivers of water (Psalm 1:3).
Of the test of a religious system: Every plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted, shall be rooted up (Matthew 15:13).
Of divided labour and undivided credit: I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase (1 Corinthians 3:6).

etymology: From Saxon bycgan, to buy. Hebrew qanah means to acquire, and also to create or possess — it is the verb in Eve's naming of Cain and in wisdom's claim that the LORD possessed her in the beginning. Greek agorazō is to buy in the agora, the market place, and is the New Testament's word for redemption at a price.
biblical_def: Buying in Scripture is the plain commercial act, and then the figure by which redemption is stated. Wisdom's counsel makes some purchases one-way: “Buy the truth, and sell it not; also wisdom, and instruction, and understanding” (Proverbs 23:23) — truth may be bought at any cost and must never be traded back. The Lord Jesus makes the kingdom worth the whole estate: the man who found treasure hid in a field “for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field” (Matthew 13:44) — and it is the joy, not the calculation, that carries the sentence. To a church rich in its own eyes He offers terms it cannot negotiate: “I counsel thee to buy of me gold tried in the fire, that thou mayest be rich” (Revelation 3:18) — buying from Christ who sells without money and without price. And Paul states the transaction that governs the believer's body: “ye are not your own... ye are bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:19-20). The doctrine is exact. Redemption is not rescue merely but purchase; a price was named and paid, the property changed hands, and the Christian's obligation follows from ownership rather than from gratitude alone.
webster_summary: To acquire the property of anything by paying a price; to purchase. In Scripture, buying the truth and never selling it, selling all to buy the field with the treasure, buying of Christ gold tried in the fire, and the believer bought with a price and therefore not his own.
webster_full: BUY, v.t. 1. To acquire the property, right or title to anything by paying a consideration or an equivalent in money.
2. To procure by a consideration given, or by something that is deemed worth the thing bought.
3. To bribe; to corrupt by money; as, to buy a man's vote.
4. From Saxon bycgan, to buy; Hebrew qanah, to acquire or possess.
5. In Scripture, buy the truth, and sell it not, Prov. 23; ye are bought with a price, 1 Cor. 6.
corruption_summary: The purchase language of redemption is emptied, so that the cross becomes a demonstration of love rather than the payment of a price; and where the price is retained, the ownership it establishes over the believer's body is quietly dropped.
corruption_paragraphs: “Bought with a price” is commercial language the Holy Ghost chose deliberately, and every theory of the atonement that removes the payment removes the word's meaning. The moral-influence theory, from Abelard to modern progressive evangelicalism, makes the cross a display of divine love intended to move men to repentance; the governmental theory makes it a demonstration that God takes sin seriously without actually satisfying justice. Both leave the sinner unpurchased and the justice of God unsatisfied. Scripture speaks of a ransom, a price, a redemption, a propitiation, and a definite people obtained: Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us; He purchased the church with His own blood. Take away the transaction and the language collapses into metaphor, and with it the believer's security, since a demonstration guarantees nobody.

The other half is dropped even more often. Paul's conclusion from the purchase is immediate and physical: your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost, ye are not your own, therefore glorify God in your body. The argument is about fornication, and it settles the matter on the ground of ownership rather than harm. That is precisely the ground the age refuses. The reigning sexual ethic rests on consent between owners of themselves, and against it the Christian claim is not that certain acts are harmful but that the believer does not own the body performing them. The principle to recover is the whole transaction: a price was named, the price was paid, the property was transferred, and the deed is in the hands of the Redeemer.
roots_summary: Hebrew qanah, to acquire, buy, or possess; ga'al, to redeem by right of kinship; Greek agorazō, to buy in the market, and exagorazō, to buy out or redeem.
roots_lines: Hebrew qanah (H7069) — to acquire, purchase, possess; “buy the truth, and sell it not” (Proverbs 23:23).
Hebrew ga'al (H1350) — to redeem by kinsman's right; the verb behind Boaz's purchase of Ruth's inheritance.
Greek agorazō (G59) — to buy in the market place; used of the redeemed purchased unto God by blood (Revelation 5:9).
Greek exagorazō (G1805) — to buy out, to redeem from; “redeemed us from the curse of the law” (Galatians 3:13).
Greek timē (G5092) — a price or value; the word in “ye are bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:20).
usage: Of the one purchase never to be reversed: Buy the truth, and sell it not (Proverbs 23:23).
Of joy that makes the cost light: for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field (Matthew 13:44).
Of the believer's ownership: ye are bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:20).

For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's.

etymology: From Saxon syllan, to give, deliver, or sell. Hebrew makar is to sell, and is used with terrible force of God selling a disobedient people into the hand of their enemies — a transfer of possession that is also a judgment.
biblical_def: Selling in Scripture exposes what a man values, because a sale reveals the seller's estimate of what he parted with. Esau's bargain is the standing example: “And Jacob said, Sell me this day thy birthright” (Genesis 25:31) — and the epistle to the Hebrews calls him a profane person who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright, which is what every sale of the eternal for the immediate amounts to. The rich young ruler is met at exactly the point where his estimate lay: “If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven” (Matthew 19:21) — a command that exposed a god, and the man went away sorrowful. In the parable the merchant sells with joy, not grief: “when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it” (Matthew 13:46). And Ananias sold honestly and lied about the price: “a certain man named Ananias, with Sapphira his wife, sold a possession” (Acts 5:1) — the sin was not in selling or in keeping back part, as Peter says plainly, but in the pretence. Selling is therefore a moral disclosure. What a man will part with, what he will not, and what he will lie about, together make a fair account of his heart.
webster_summary: To transfer property to another for an equivalent in money; to part with for a price. In Scripture, Esau selling his birthright, the ruler commanded to sell what he had, the merchant who sold all for one pearl, and Ananias who sold a possession and lied about the price.
webster_full: SELL, v.t. 1. To transfer property, or the exclusive right of possession, to another for an equivalent in money.
2. To make a matter of bargain and sale; to accept a price or reward for; as, to sell one's honour.
3. To betray for a consideration; as, Judas sold his Master.
4. From Saxon syllan, to deliver, to give over; Hebrew makar, to sell.
5. In Scripture, sell me this day thy birthright, Gen. 25; sold all that he had, and bought it, Matt. 13.
corruption_summary: The command to the rich young ruler is universalised into a rule that possessions are sinful, or else neutralised entirely so that it asks nothing of anyone; and generosity is performed for reputation, which is the sin Ananias died for.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite mishandlings of Matthew 19:21 are common. Liberation theology and its evangelical imitators universalise it: property is inherently oppressive, and the gospel is a programme of redistribution, so that a man's standing before God is measured by his economics. Scripture forbids the generalisation — Abraham, Job, Lydia, and Philemon were all people of means, believers are commanded to provide for their own houses, and the eighth commandment presupposes lawful property. The opposite evasion is more comfortable and just as false: because the command was addressed to one man, it is treated as asking nothing of anyone now. But the Lord aimed at the ruler's god, and He still does. The question the passage puts is not whether every Christian must liquidate but what a man would refuse Christ if He asked for it — and most men know the answer before they finish the sentence.

Ananias is the other warning, and Peter's words remove every excuse from it: whiles it remained, was it not thine own? and after it was sold, was it not in thine own power? The property was his, the sale was voluntary, and the amount given was entirely at his discretion. What killed him was the performance — the appearance of a total gift where a partial one had been made, generosity staged for the admiration of the church. That sin is not extinct; it has merely acquired better instruments, since giving can now be publicised at scale. The principle to recover is our Lord's own in Matthew 6: let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth. Real generosity is answerable to God, who sees in secret, and needs no witnesses at all.
roots_summary: Hebrew makar, to sell, and figuratively to deliver over in judgment; mimkar, a sale or thing sold; Greek pōleō, to sell, and pipraskoo, to sell, especially into slavery.
roots_lines: Hebrew makar (H4376) — to sell; used of Joseph sold by his brethren and of Israel sold into the hand of her enemies (Judges 2:14).
Hebrew mimkar (H4465) — a sale, or the thing sold; governed in Israel by the jubilee laws of Leviticus 25.
Greek pōleō (G4453) — to sell; the verb of the merchant who sold all for the pearl (Matthew 13:46).
Greek pipraskoo (G4097) — to sell, often into bondage; “sold under sin” (Romans 7:14).
Greek bēbēlos (G952) — profane, unhallowed; the epithet given Esau for selling his birthright (Hebrews 12:16).

Of a command that exposed an idol: go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor (Matthew 19:21).
Of joyful, total exchange: went and sold all that he had, and bought it (Matthew 13:46).

etymology: From French payer, Latin pacare, to appease or satisfy, from pax, peace — to pay is to make peace with a claim. Hebrew shalam carries the same idea and the same root as shalom: to make whole, to complete, to render what restores the balance.
biblical_def: Payment in Scripture is the completion of an obligation, and the Bible is severe about obligations that are contracted lightly. Vows come first: “When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed” (Ecclesiastes 5:4), and the Psalmist joins payment to worship itself — “Offer unto God thanksgiving; and pay thy vows unto the most High” (Psalm 50:14). Civil obligation is treated with the same seriousness: “For this cause pay ye tribute also: for they are God's ministers, attending continually upon this very thing” (Romans 13:6) — taxes are paid to men who are, whether they know it or not, ministers of God. And the parable of the unmerciful servant sets the whole matter in the light of the gospel: the lord “commanded him to be sold, and his wife, and children, and all that he had, and payment to be made” (Matthew 18:25) — a debt of ten thousand talents, entirely beyond payment, forgiven outright, after which the forgiven man took his fellowservant by the throat over a hundred pence. The doctrine is plain: God requires that men pay what they owe; and He knows that the debt every man owes Him could never be paid, which is why the gospel is not an easier payment plan but a cancelled account and a new heart to match.
webster_summary: To discharge a debt; to render what is due; to satisfy a claim. In Scripture, the command to pay what is vowed and not defer it, to pay vows unto the most High, to pay tribute to the civil ruler as God's minister, and the debtor commanded to be sold that payment might be made.
webster_full: PAY, v.t. 1. To discharge a debt; to deliver to a creditor the value of a debt, in money or in goods.
2. To compensate; to requite; to make amends for; as, to pay a man for his labour.
3. To render what is due to a superior; as, to pay homage, to pay tribute, to pay vows.
4. From French payer, Latin pacare, to appease or satisfy, from pax, peace.
5. In Scripture, pay that which thou hast vowed, Eccl. 5; for this cause pay ye tribute also, Rom. 13.
corruption_summary: Vows and obligations are treated as expressions of present feeling rather than binding commitments, so that a man may walk away from what he swore; and the forgiveness of an unpayable debt is received without the mercy toward others it was meant to produce.
corruption_paragraphs: Ecclesiastes 5 warns against the mouth that is rash before God, and the culture has industrialised rashness. Vows — marital, membership, ordination, financial — are increasingly understood as statements of current intention that lapse when the feeling changes, and the language of authenticity is used to dignify the retreat: to keep a vow one no longer feels would be dishonest. Scripture takes the contrary view throughout. Psalm 15 marks out the man who sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not, as one who shall abide in God's tabernacle. It is precisely when a vow costs what was not anticipated that keeping it becomes worship. The Preacher's counsel is not that vows are unwise but that they are serious: better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.

The unmerciful servant sets the second corruption before us in a form nobody can miss. He was forgiven ten thousand talents — an absurd, unpayable sum, chosen precisely because no servant could ever have owed or repaid it — and then throttled a fellowservant over a hundred pence. The parable is the Lord's exposition of the petition He had just taught: forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. It does not teach that a man earns pardon by forgiving; it teaches that a man who has really received pardon of that size cannot hold a hundred pence against his brother, and that where he does, his profession is exposed. The principle to recover joins both halves of the entry: pay what you owe to men, and remember what has been cancelled for you by God.
roots_summary: Hebrew shalam, to make whole, complete, or repay, from the same root as shalom; nathan, to give; Greek apodidōmi, to give back or render, and tinō, to pay a penalty.
roots_lines: Hebrew shalam (H7999) — to be complete, to make good, to repay; the root of shalom, peace as wholeness restored.
Hebrew neder (H5088) — a vow; the voluntary obligation Ecclesiastes 5 commands men to pay without delay.
Greek apodidōmi (G591) — to give back, render, repay; “render therefore to all their dues” (Romans 13:7).
Greek opheilē (G3782) — a debt, that which is owed; the word behind “forgive us our debts.”
Greek talanton (G5007) — a talent, a very large weight of silver; ten thousand of them is the unpayable debt of Matthew 18:24.
usage: Of vows kept without delay: pay that which thou hast vowed (Ecclesiastes 5:4).
Of civil obligation as a duty to God: For this cause pay ye tribute also: for they are God's ministers (Romans 13:6).
Of a debt beyond all payment: commanded him to be sold... and payment to be made (Matthew 18:25).

etymology: From Saxon wascan. Hebrew distinguishes what English merges: rachats is to wash the body, kabas is to wash clothes by treading or beating them. Greek keeps a similar distinction: louō is to bathe the whole body, niptō to wash a part, and the difference carries real doctrine in John 13.
biblical_def: Washing runs through Scripture as the standing figure for cleansing from sin, and the Bible is careful to say who does it. David does not offer to wash himself: “Wash me throughly from mine iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin” (Psalm 51:2). Isaiah's command to wash is immediately explained as repentance and the abandoning of evil doings: “Wash you, make you clean; put away the evil of your doings from before mine eyes; cease to do evil” (Isaiah 1:16). The Lord Jesus, kneeling with a towel, makes the washing of feet the sign of an absolute necessity: “If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me” (John 13:8) — and when Peter overcorrects and asks for his hands and head too, the answer draws the great distinction: he that is bathed needeth only to wash his feet. And Ananias puts it to Saul as a summons that will not wait: “arise, and be baptized, and wash away thy sins, calling on the name of the Lord” (Acts 22:16). Taken together the passages hold the whole doctrine: the bath of regeneration happens once and is God's work; the daily washing of defiled feet is the ongoing confession of a man already clean; and no one washes himself into a standing with God.
webster_summary: To cleanse by water or other liquid; to purify. In Scripture, the prayer to be washed throughly from iniquity, the command to wash and put away evil doings, Christ's word that unless He washes a man he has no part with Him, and the summons to be baptized and wash away sins.
webster_full: WASH, v.t. 1. To cleanse by ablution, or by rubbing in water; to free from dirt or filth by water.
2. To overflow or dash upon; as, waves washing the shore.
3. To purify from guilt or defilement; to cleanse morally.
4. From Saxon wascan; Hebrew rachats, to wash the body, and kabas, to wash garments.
5. In Scripture, wash me throughly from mine iniquity, Ps. 51; if I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me, John 13.
corruption_summary: Baptismal washing is made the instrument that itself removes sin, so that the sign is confused with the thing signified; and, in reaction, the daily washing of a believer's defilement is neglected as though confession were unnecessary once a man is justified.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 22:16 is the standing proof text for baptismal regeneration, and the reading has to ignore the rest of Scripture to stand. Cornelius received the Holy Ghost before he was baptized; the thief on the cross went to paradise unbaptized; Abraham was justified by faith and received circumcision afterward as a seal of the righteousness he already had. Baptism is a sign and seal of the washing away of sins, and Scripture regularly speaks of the sign in the language of the thing signified, exactly as it says the cup is the new testament in His blood. What washes is the blood of Christ applied by the Spirit — unto him that loved us, and washed us from our sins in his own blood. The water preaches that, seals it to the believer, and never replaces it. Where the sign is made the instrument, men are sent to the font instead of to Christ.

The opposite neglect is the more common failure among the sound. John 13 distinguishes the bath from the foot-washing: the disciple who is bathed is clean every whit and does not need bathing again, but his feet get dirty walking, and they must be washed. That is the doctrine of daily confession in a picture. Justification is once for all and cannot be repeated; fellowship is disturbed by sin and is restored by confession, since if we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us. A believer who ignores his feet on the ground that he is already bathed will find his communion cold and his conscience dull, and he will have no explanation for it. The principle to recover keeps both: one bath, many washings, and Christ Himself kneeling with the basin.
roots_summary: Hebrew rachats, to wash the body; kabas, to wash garments by treading; Greek louō, to bathe wholly, niptō, to wash a part, and apolouō, to wash away.
roots_lines: Hebrew rachats (H7364) — to wash or bathe the body; the priests washed at the laver before serving (Exodus 30:19-21).
Hebrew kabas (H3526) — to wash clothes by treading or beating; used in Psalm 51:2, “wash me throughly.”
Greek louō (G3068) — to bathe the whole body; “he that is washed needeth not save to wash his feet” (John 13:10).
Greek niptō (G3538) — to wash a part of the body; the foot-washing of John 13.
Greek apolouō (G628) — to wash away, wash off; “wash away thy sins” (Acts 22:16) and “ye are washed” (1 Corinthians 6:11).
usage: Of cleansing sought from God alone: Wash me throughly from mine iniquity (Psalm 51:2).
Of the necessity of Christ's cleansing: If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me (John 13:8).
Of the summons to the new convert: arise, and be baptized, and wash away thy sins (Acts 22:16).
scriptures: Psalm 51:2
Wash me throughly from mine iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin.
Isaiah 1:16
Wash you, make you clean; put away the evil of your doings from before mine eyes; cease to do evil;
John 13:8
Peter saith unto him, Thou shalt never wash my feet. Jesus answered him, If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me.
Acts 22:16
And now why tarriest thou? arise, and be baptized, and wash away thy sins, calling on the name of the Lord.

etymology: Of uncertain origin, perhaps from Welsh bwrw, to cast or shed. Hebrew shaphak is to pour out, spill, or shed — used of blood, of wrath, of the soul in prayer — and yatsaq is to pour as one pours oil in anointing. Both keep the idea of emptying a vessel completely.
biblical_def: Pouring in Scripture is emptying without reserve, and it is used of God and of men in ways that answer one another. God pours out His Spirit: “I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy” (Joel 2:28), the prophecy Peter claimed at Pentecost. He pours out blessing beyond capacity: “prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it” (Malachi 3:10). The Servant pours out Himself: “he hath poured out his soul unto death: and he was numbered with the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12) — the atonement described as a vessel emptied to the last. And the believer is invited to do the one thing he can: “Trust in him at all times; ye people, pour out your heart before him: God is a refuge for us” (Psalm 62:8). The pattern is worth marking. Every pouring in Scripture is total — the Spirit not measured out, the blessing beyond room, the soul unto death, the heart held back in nothing — and the reserve that characterises most religion is exactly what the word excludes.
webster_summary: To cause to flow out of a vessel; to send forth in a stream; to empty out. In Scripture, God pouring out His Spirit upon all flesh, pouring out a blessing beyond room to receive it, the Servant pouring out His soul unto death, and the believer commanded to pour out his heart before God.
webster_full: POUR, v.t. 1. To cause to flow, as a liquid; to send forth from a vessel.
2. To emit; to send forth in a stream or continued succession.
3. To send forth freely; as, to pour out one's complaint or one's heart.
4. Perhaps from the Welsh bwrw, to cast, to shed; Hebrew shaphak, to pour out.
5. In Scripture, I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh, Joel 2; he hath poured out his soul unto death, Isa. 53.
corruption_summary: The outpouring of the Spirit is claimed as a repeatable event men can schedule, and Malachi's promise of poured-out blessing is converted into a contract by which giving obliges God to enrich the giver.
corruption_paragraphs: Malachi 3:10 has become the most-quoted verse in prosperity preaching, and the abuse is worth stating precisely, because the verse does teach something real. God addresses a nation under a covenant with tangible sanctions, charges it with robbing Him in tithes and offerings, and promises agricultural blessing on repentance — opened windows, a rebuked devourer, a fruitful vine. What the prosperity teacher does is lift the promise out of that covenant, attach it to individual giving in a new-covenant church, and guarantee financial return in proportion to the gift. That is not faith but investment, and it makes God a debtor to men. Scripture's new-covenant teaching on giving is different in kind: give cheerfully, not grudgingly nor of necessity; sow bountifully and God will supply seed to the sower; and the God who did not spare His own Son will freely give us all things — none of which is a mechanism for enrichment.

The outpouring of the Spirit suffers a parallel corruption. Joel's prophecy was claimed by Peter at Pentecost as fulfilled — this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel — and the Spirit poured out then has not been withdrawn. Modern revivalism repeatedly announces fresh outpourings, schedules them, and markets them, as though Pentecost were a recurring event the church could arrange. The cessationist position the dictionary holds is not that God has stopped working powerfully, but that the sign gifts attesting the apostolic foundation have ceased with the foundation, and that the Spirit now works through the ordinary means He has appointed. The principle to recover is Psalm 62:8, which is available to any believer on any day: pour out your heart before Him, holding nothing back, for God is a refuge for us.
roots_summary: Hebrew shaphak, to pour out, spill, or shed; yatsaq, to pour as oil in anointing; 'arah, to empty out; Greek ekcheō, to pour out.
roots_lines: Hebrew shaphak (H8210) — to pour out or shed; used of blood shed, of wrath poured out, and of the soul poured out in prayer (1 Samuel 1:15).
Hebrew yatsaq (H3332) — to pour or cast; the verb of anointing oil poured on the head (1 Samuel 10:1).
Hebrew 'arah (H6168) — to make bare, to empty out; “he hath poured out his soul unto death” (Isaiah 53:12).
Greek ekcheō (G1632) — to pour out; used of the Spirit poured out at Pentecost (Acts 2:17-18).
Greek spendō (G4689) — to be poured out as a drink offering; Paul's word for his own approaching death (2 Timothy 4:6).
usage: Of the promised gift of the Spirit: I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh (Joel 2:28).
Of the atonement as total self-giving: he hath poured out his soul unto death (Isaiah 53:12).
Of prayer without reserve: ye people, pour out your heart before him (Psalm 62:8).
scriptures: Joel 2:28
And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions:
Malachi 3:10

Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it.
Isaiah 53:12

Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong; because he hath poured out his soul unto death: and he was numbered with the transgressors; and he bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
Psalm 62:8
Trust in him at all times; ye people, pour out your heart before him: God is a refuge for us. Selah.

etymology: From Saxon baernan, to consume with fire. Hebrew ba'ar means to kindle or be alight; saraph, to burn up completely — from which comes seraphim, the burning ones. Scripture uses the verb for what fire does to what it touches, and then for what God's presence and God's word do to a man.
biblical_def: Fire in Scripture destroys what is combustible and reveals what is not, and burning is therefore both the language of judgment and the language of the presence of God. The bush is the great instance of a burning that does not consume: “the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed” (Exodus 3:2), and Moses turns aside precisely because that is impossible — “I will now turn aside, and see this great sight, why the bush is not burnt” (Exodus 3:3). The altar fire was to be perpetual: “The fire shall ever be burning upon the altar; it shall never go out” (Leviticus 6:13) — a sacrifice always available, and a flame no priest was permitted to let die. Jeremiah, having resolved to stop preaching because it cost him too much, finds the word itself will not let him: “then his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay” (Jeremiah 20:9). And Paul sets the most extreme act a man could perform beneath love: “though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:3). The word therefore measures reality. God burns without consuming, His word burns in a reluctant prophet, His altar burns continually — and martyrdom itself, without love, burns to no purpose.
webster_summary: To consume with fire; to be on fire; to glow or be inflamed. In Scripture, the bush that burned and was not consumed, the fire ever burning on the altar, the word of God as a burning fire shut up in the prophet's bones, and the body given to be burned without charity profiting nothing.
webster_full: BURN, v.t. 1. To consume with fire; to reduce to ashes by the action of heat or fire.
2. To expose to the action of fire; to heat or dry, as to burn clay.
3. BURN, v.i. To be on fire; to flame; and figuratively, to be inflamed with passion or desire.
4. From Saxon baernan, to burn; Hebrew ba'ar, to kindle, and saraph, to burn up.
5. In Scripture, the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed, Exod. 3; the fire shall ever be burning upon the altar, Lev. 6.
corruption_summary: The fire of God's judgment is denied outright, so that hell is annihilation or a metaphor; and zeal is measured by heat rather than by truth, so that a burning that consumes is mistaken for a burning that sanctifies.
corruption_paragraphs: Annihilationism, now widely held among evangelicals who once rejected it, reads the fire of judgment as destroying the wicked utterly rather than punishing them consciously and for ever. The appeal of the doctrine is obvious and the exegesis is not. The same word, aiōnios, describes the life of the redeemed and the punishment of the lost in a single verse (Matthew 25:46); the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever; and the worm dieth not and the fire is not quenched, which is a strange way to describe an event that ends. The burning bush is instructive on the point Scripture presses: fire in God's hand does not require consumption. It burned and was not consumed, which is the very thing that made Moses turn aside, and it is the thing modern sentiment cannot bear to contemplate applied to the impenitent.

The second corruption is measured in the pulpit rather than in the doctrine of hell. Zeal is easily confused with fire, and a great deal of religious heat has nothing to do with the word of God burning in a man. Jeremiah's fire is worth studying because it came the wrong way round: he had decided to stop speaking, and could not, because God's own word would not lie quiet in him. That is not temperament, and it cannot be worked up. Paul's test in 1 Corinthians 13 sets the ceiling on all such intensity — a man may give his body to be burned and profit nothing. The principle to recover is that fire is a servant of truth and love, never a substitute for them, and that the altar fire the priests were commanded to keep burning was kept by ordinary men putting on wood every morning.
roots_summary: Hebrew ba'ar, to kindle or burn; saraph, to burn up wholly, whence seraphim; qatar, to burn incense; Greek kaiō, to burn, and katakaiō, to burn up.
roots_lines: Hebrew ba'ar (H1197) — to kindle, to be alight; the burning bush and the burning anger of the LORD.
Hebrew saraph (H8313) — to burn completely; the root behind seraphim, the burning ones of Isaiah 6.
Hebrew qatar (H6999) — to burn incense or a sacrifice into smoke; the priestly verb of the altar.
Greek kaiō (G2545) — to burn or be lit; “let your loins be girded about, and your lights burning” (Luke 12:35).
Greek katakaiō (G2618) — to burn up utterly; the chaff burned with unquenchable fire (Matthew 3:12).
usage: Of God's presence that burns without consuming: the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed (Exodus 3:2).
Of the perpetual altar: The fire shall ever be burning upon the altar; it shall never go out (Leviticus 6:13).
Of the word that will not be silenced: his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones (Jeremiah 20:9).
scriptures: Exodus 3:2
And the angel of the LORD appeared unto him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush: and he looked, and, behold, the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed.
Exodus 3:3
And Moses said, I will now turn aside, and see this great sight, why the bush is not burnt.
Leviticus 6:13
The fire shall ever be burning upon the altar; it shall never go out.
Jeremiah 20:9

Then I said, I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name. But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay.

etymology: From Saxon brecan, to break, cognate with Latin frango. Hebrew shabar is to break in pieces; parar, to break a covenant or frustrate a purpose — the same verb for smashing a vessel and for violating an oath, which is the Hebrew way of saying that a broken promise is a broken thing.
biblical_def: Scripture distinguishes sharply between the breaking God requires and the breaking He refuses to do. What He requires is the heart: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise” (Psalm 51:17) — the one offering a sinner can bring that will not be turned away. What He refuses is the weak: “A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench, till he send forth judgment unto victory” (Matthew 12:20) — a Messiah who does not finish off what is already damaged. What He does to the hard is another matter entirely: “Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?” (Jeremiah 23:29) — the same word that binds up a broken heart shatters a proud one. And the church's central act carries the word into worship: the first believers “continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers” (Acts 2:42), where the breaking of bread recalls a body broken deliberately for others. The doctrine is a single line: God breaks the proud with His word, refuses to break the bruised, receives the broken heart as sacrifice, and gives His own broken body as the ground of it all.
webster_summary: To part by violence; to burst or shatter; to violate, as a covenant; to break bread. In Scripture, the broken and contrite heart God will not despise, the bruised reed He will not break, His word as a hammer that breaks the rock, and the breaking of bread in the church's steadfast practice.
webster_full: BREAK, v.t. 1. To part or divide by force and violence; to sever; to burst; to shatter.
2. To violate, as a contract or promise; as, to break faith, to break a covenant.
3. To tame; to subdue; to make tractable; as, to break a horse or a stubborn will.
4. From Saxon brecan; Latin frango, fregi, to break.
5. In Scripture, a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise, Ps. 51; a bruised reed shall he not break, Matt. 12.
corruption_summary: Brokenness is aestheticised into a mood of general woundedness that requires no repentance, so that a word Scripture reserves for contrition over sin is used for suffering in general.
corruption_paragraphs: “Brokenness” has become a favourite word in the modern church, and it has quietly changed meaning. In David's Psalm the broken spirit is a man who has sinned against God, been confronted by a prophet, and come to the end of his defences: against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight. The brokenness now commonly described is a state of woundedness — the pain of what has been done to a person rather than sorrow for what he has done to God — and the two are not the same, however genuinely both may hurt. Scripture has abundant tenderness for the afflicted; the smoking flax is not quenched, and the Man of sorrows is acquainted with grief. But contrition is a specific thing, it names sin as sin, and it is the sacrifice God accepts. A church that speaks constantly of brokenness and rarely of repentance has kept the vocabulary and lost the doctrine.

The second matter is the misuse of Matthew 12:20 to forbid all severity. The bruised reed is not broken, and no faithful minister should ever break one — but the same Lord who spoke that word wove a scourge of small cords, called Herod a fox, and told the Pharisees they were whited sepulchres. Jeremiah 23:29 is the necessary companion text: God's word is a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces, and rocks are what proud hearts are. Discernment consists in knowing which is in front of you. To use the hammer on a bruised reed is cruelty; to offer a bruised reed's comfort to a rock is flattery, and it leaves the man unbroken and unsaved. The principle to recover is that both instruments are in Scripture and both belong to love.
roots_summary: Hebrew shabar, to break in pieces; dakah, to crush or be contrite; parar, to break a covenant; Greek klaō, to break bread, and syntribō, to shatter.
roots_lines: Hebrew shabar (H7665) — to break, shatter, or rend; used of vessels, of bones, and of a broken heart (Psalm 34:18).
Hebrew dakah (H1794) — to crush, to be contrite; the root of the contrite heart in Psalm 51:17.
Hebrew parar (H6565) — to break or frustrate, especially a covenant (Genesis 17:14).
Greek klaō (G2806) — to break, used exclusively of breaking bread in the New Testament (Acts 2:42; 20:7).
Greek syntribō (G4937) — to break in pieces, to crush; “a bruised reed shall he not break” (Matthew 12:20).
usage: Of the sacrifice God accepts: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise (Psalm 51:17).
Of the tenderness of Messiah: A bruised reed shall he not break (Matthew 12:20).
Of the word that shatters pride: like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces (Jeremiah 23:29).
scriptures: Psalm 51:17
The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.
Matthew 12:20
A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench, till he send forth judgment unto victory.
Jeremiah 23:29
Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?
Acts 2:42

etymology: From Saxon bindan, to tie. Hebrew 'asar is to bind or imprison; chabash is to bind up, as a wound is bandaged or a turban wound about the head — the same verb for restraining and for healing, since both are done with a cord.
biblical_def: Binding in Scripture is either restraint or repair, and God does both. He binds up: “He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds” (Psalm 147:3) — the surgeon's work, done by a God who is elsewhere described as counting the stars in the same passage, so that the immensity and the tenderness stand side by side. The believer is commanded to bind the word where it cannot be mislaid: “thou shalt bind them for a sign upon thine hand, and they shall be as frontlets between thine eyes” (Deuteronomy 6:8), and Solomon presses the same instruction inward: “Bind them continually upon thine heart, and tie them about thy neck” (Proverbs 6:21). And the Lord Jesus gives His church an authority stated in the language of binding: “whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matthew 16:19) — the same words repeated to the whole body in Matthew 18 in the context of church discipline. Binding is therefore an act of authority, of memory, and of mercy. A cord fastens a bandage to a wound, a commandment to a hand, and a judgment to a case; and in every instance what is bound is held where it will not slip.
webster_summary: To tie together or confine with a cord; to bind up, as a wound; to lay under obligation. In Scripture, God binding up the wounds of the broken in heart, the word bound as a sign upon the hand and continually upon the heart, and the keys by which what the church binds on earth is bound in heaven.
webster_full: BIND, v.t. 1. To tie together, or confine with a cord, chain, or anything that is flexible.
2. To gird, inwrap or involve; to confine by a bandage; as, to bind up a wound.
3. To oblige by a promise, vow, stipulation, covenant, law or duty.
4. From Saxon bindan; Hebrew 'asar, to bind, and chabash, to bind up or bandage.
5. In Scripture, bindeth up their wounds, Ps. 147; whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, Matt. 16.
corruption_summary: The keys of binding and loosing are claimed as a personal power over souls, whether by a hierarchy or by teachers who bind Satan and loose blessings at will; and the plain command to bind God's word on the heart is reduced to external tokens.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 16:19 has been pulled in two directions, both of them away from the text. Rome takes the keys as a personal grant to Peter and his successors, so that a hierarchy holds the power of admission to heaven and the forgiveness of sins is dispensed through its officers. But the Lord repeats the identical binding-and-loosing formula in Matthew 18:18 to the assembled church in the context of a disciplinary case — tell it unto the church — and the apostles never exercise anything like a personal power of absolution. The keys are the authority to declare the terms of the kingdom as Christ has given them: the gospel preached, professing believers received, the impenitent put out. What heaven ratifies is a judgment made according to Christ's word, not a decree invented by His servants; a church that binds where He has not bound binds nothing at all.

The other misuse is charismatic rather than hierarchical: binding Satan, binding spirits over cities, and loosing blessings, healing, or finances by declaration. There is no instance in the New Testament of any believer binding the devil by such a formula, and the epistles — written to churches in every kind of trouble — never once instruct Christians to do it; they say resist the devil, put on the whole armour of God, and be sober and vigilant. Meanwhile the plain command is neglected. Deuteronomy 6:8 tells a man to bind the word on his hand and Proverbs 6:21 to bind it on his heart, and the Pharisees kept the first by widening their phylacteries while breaking the second. The principle to recover is that God's word bound to the heart governs the hand, and no amount of external binding substitutes for it.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'asar, to bind or imprison; chabash, to bind up, bandage, or gird; qashar, to tie or conspire; Greek deō, to bind, and luō, to loose.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'asar (H631) — to bind, tie, or imprison; used of Samson bound and of a vow that binds the soul (Numbers 30:2).
Hebrew chabash (H2280) — to bind up, bandage, or wrap; “bindeth up their wounds” (Psalm 147:3).
Hebrew qashar (H7194) — to tie or bind together; “bind them continually upon thine heart” (Proverbs 6:21).
Greek deō (G1210) — to bind; used of binding on earth what is bound in heaven (Matthew 16:19; 18:18).
Greek luō (G3089) — to loose, release, or dissolve; the counterpart of deō in the keys.
usage: Of God's healing of the broken: He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds (Psalm 147:3).
Of the word fastened to the memory: thou shalt bind them for a sign upon thine hand (Deuteronomy 6:8).
Of the church's declared authority: whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven (Matthew 16:19).

He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds.
Deuteronomy 6:8
And thou shalt bind them for a sign upon thine hand, and they shall be as frontlets between thine eyes.
Proverbs 6:21
Bind them continually upon thine heart, and tie them about thy neck.
Matthew 16:19
And I will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.
